questions.stem: According to the sliding filament theory, contraction shortens a sarcomere because
options: actin and myosin filaments themselves shorten
thin filaments slide over thick filaments
questions.explanation: Filament lengths stay the same; actin slides on myosin so I and H bands narrow.

questions.stem: A sarcomere is the segment of a myofibril lying between two successive
questions.explanation: Z lines (Z discs) bound each sarcomere, the functional unit of striated muscle.

questions.stem: Calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum bind to
questions.explanation: Ca2+–troponin shifts tropomyosin so myosin-binding sites on actin are exposed.

questions.stem: Amoeboid movement in humans is typically shown by
questions.explanation: Phagocytes crawl by pseudopodia; sperm use flagella and the trachea uses cilia.

questions.stem: Human cardiac muscle fibres are
questions.explanation: Heart muscle has striations and intercalated discs but is not under conscious control.

questions.stem: Red skeletal muscle fibres appear dark because they are rich in
questions.explanation: Myoglobin stores O2 and many mitochondria support aerobic, fatigue-resistant contraction.

questions.stem: The adult human skeleton contains about 206 bones. The axial skeleton includes the
options: skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs
questions.explanation: Axial = skull + vertebral column + sternum + ribs (80 bones); the rest is appendicular.

questions.stem: The shoulder joint is an example of a
questions.explanation: The humeral head fits the glenoid cavity, allowing movement in many planes.

questions.stem: Gouty arthritis is caused by accumulation of crystals of
questions.explanation: Urate crystals inflame joints, classically the great toe.

questions.stem: Of the twelve pairs of ribs, the last two pairs are called floating ribs because they
options: do not attach to the sternum even through cartilage
are fused to the cervical vertebrae
questions.explanation: Pairs 11 and 12 have no sternal attachment; 1–7 are true ribs and 8–10 are false (vertebrochondral).

questions.stem: During contraction the A band length remains almost constant while the H zone
questions.explanation: A band is the myosin length; H is the myosin-only middle that is covered as actin slides in.

questions.stem: The I band of a sarcomere contains
questions.explanation: I (isotropic) band is thin filaments on either side of the Z line; A is the anisotropic myosin-containing band.

questions.stem: Rigor mortis occurs after death because ATP is no longer available to
options: pump Ca2+ into the extracellular fluid only
questions.explanation: Without ATP, cross-bridges stay locked; muscles stiffen until proteins begin to decay.

questions.stem: Which event is essential for the power stroke of a myosin head?
options: Hydrolysis of ATP and release of ADP + Pi after binding actin
Binding of Ca2+ to myosin directly
Shortening of the myosin thick filament
Removal of all ATP from the fibre
questions.explanation: ATP hydrolysis cocks the head; actin binding and product release produce the stroke.

questions.stem: The M line of a sarcomere is the
options: mid-line that holds thick filaments in the A band
same structure as a Z line
questions.explanation: M-line proteins interconnect myosin filaments at the centre of the A band.

questions.stem: An action potential spreading into T-tubules causes the sarcoplasmic reticulum to
options: take up all Na+ from the fibre
release stored Ca2+ into the sarcoplasm
questions.explanation: Voltage sensors on T-tubules open SR Ca2+ channels, starting contraction.

questions.stem: Ciliary movement in humans helps to
options: propel mucus in the respiratory tract and ova in the oviduct
slide actin on myosin in the heart
questions.explanation: Coordinated cilia clear the airways and move the egg toward the uterus.

questions.stem: Smooth muscle differs from skeletal muscle in being
options: attached to bones by tendons only
questions.explanation: Visceral muscle has no sarcomere striations and is autonomic.

questions.stem: White muscle fibres, compared with red fibres, typically
options: have more myoglobin and tire slowly
have less myoglobin and tire quickly
are found only in the heart
questions.explanation: Pale fibres rely more on anaerobic glycolysis and are used for short, fast bursts.

questions.stem: The pectoral girdle of each side is formed by the
questions.explanation: Collar bone and shoulder blade suspend the upper limb; the pelvic girdle is hip bones.

questions.stem: Sutures of the skull are examples of
questions.explanation: Fibrous joints allow almost no movement; synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity.

questions.stem: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder that affects
questions.explanation: Antibodies impair acetylcholine receptors, causing muscle weakness and fatigue.

questions.stem: The vertebral formula of the adult human column (cervical–thoracic–lumbar–sacral–coccygeal bones) is
options: C7 T12 L5 S1 Co1 (26 bones)
questions.explanation: Seven cervical, twelve thoracic and five lumbar vertebrae plus fused sacrum and coccyx give 26 bones.

questions.stem: Which statement about sliding filaments is correct?
options: Both A and I bands shorten equally
Thin filaments slide inward; A band width stays the same
Thick filaments slide into the Z line and vanish
questions.explanation: Myosin length (A) is constant; overlap increases so I and H shrink.

questions.stem: Which pairing of sarcomere region and contents is incorrect?
options: A band — myosin with overlapping actin in parts
Z line — attachment of thin filaments
questions.explanation: The H zone is the central myosin-only part of the A band, not actin.

questions.stem: Identify the incorrect step in excitation–contraction coupling.
options: Acetylcholine at the motor end-plate depolarises the fibre
Ca2+ binds tropomyosin directly and covers the active sites
ATP is needed both for the power stroke cycle and to pump Ca2+ back
questions.explanation: Ca2+ binds troponin, not tropomyosin; tropomyosin then moves off the active sites.
